title: The male system: testes and scrotum
summary: Gonads, ducts, glands and supports; why the testes hang outside; and what is inside one.
objectives: List the gonads, ducts, accessory glands and supporting structures of the male system
Explain how the scrotum keeps the testes cool
Describe the coverings and internal plan of the testis
takeaways: Testis → epididymis → ductus deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra.
Accessory glands: paired seminal vesicles, single prostate, paired bulbourethral glands.
Sperm need about 35 °C; dartos (smooth) and cremaster (skeletal) pull the testes up in the cold.
Seminiferous tubules → tubuli recti → rete testis → efferent ductules → epididymis.

steps.title: The plan of the male system
steps.text:
The gonads are the paired testes, which make sperm (the male gametes) and testosterone. Sperm leave through a duct system: epididymis → ductus deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra, which in males is shared with the urinary system.

Three accessory glands add fluid: the paired seminal vesicles, the single prostate and the paired bulbourethral glands. The scrotum, spermatic cord and penis support and deliver.

check.q: Name the male duct system in order.
check.a: Epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra.

steps.title: Keeping cool: the scrotum
steps.text:
The testes hang outside the body cavity in the scrotum because sperm production needs a temperature of about 35 °C, a few degrees below core.

The dartos muscle, smooth muscle in the scrotal wall, wrinkles the skin and contracts in the cold to draw the testes up; it relaxes when warm. The cremaster muscle, skeletal muscle in the spermatic cord, also lifts the testis.

check.q: Which scrotal muscle is smooth muscle, and what does it do in the cold?
check.a: The dartos: it contracts, wrinkling the skin and drawing the testes toward the body.

steps.title: Inside the testis
steps.text:
A serous sac, the tunica vaginalis, surrounds the front and sides of each testis. Beneath it the tough tunica albuginea sends septa inward, dividing the testis into lobules of tightly coiled seminiferous tubules.

Sperm leave the tubules through a short tubulus rectus (straight tubule) into the rete testis, then through efferent ductules into the head of the epididymis.

check.q: Trace sperm from the seminiferous tubule to the epididymis.
check.a: Seminiferous tubule → tubulus rectus → rete testis → efferent ductules → epididymis.

practice.q: Trace sperm out of the testis
Which accessory gland is single (unpaired)?
practice.why: Seminal vesicles and bulbourethral glands are paired.

practice.q: Why are the testes in the scrotum?
practice.a: Spermatogenesis needs about 35 °C, a few degrees below core body temperature.

practice.q: What divides the testis into lobules?
practice.a: Septa from the tunica albuginea.

title: Spermatogenesis and the sperm cell
summary: From stem cell at the tubule wall to swimming sperm in the lumen, and what each part of a sperm does.
objectives: Identify seminiferous tubules, interstitial cells and sustentacular cells
List the cell stages of spermatogenesis and where mitosis and meiosis occur
Describe spermiogenesis and the structure of a sperm
takeaways: Leydig (interstitial) cells make testosterone; Sertoli (sustentacular) cells nurse germ cells and form the blood–testis barrier.
Spermatogonium → (mitosis) primary spermatocyte → (meiosis I) secondary spermatocyte → (meiosis II) spermatid → (spermiogenesis) sperm.
Meiosis halves the chromosomes: diploid to haploid gametes.
Head (nucleus + acrosome), midpiece (mitochondria), tail (flagellum).

steps.title: A tubule in cross-section
steps.text:
Each seminiferous tubule is where sperm are made. Between tubules, small clusters of interstitial (Leydig) cells sit in the connective tissue and secrete testosterone.

Tall sustentacular (Sertoli) cells reach from the basement membrane to the lumen. They support and nourish the developing cells, move them inward, and their tight junctions form the blood–testis barrier, hiding the genetically new germ cells from the immune system.

check.q: Which cells secrete testosterone, and where are they?
check.a: Interstitial (Leydig) cells, between the seminiferous tubules.

steps.title: Mitosis, then meiosis
steps.text:
Spermatogonia, diploid stem cells against the basement membrane, divide by mitosis. Some become primary spermatocytes, which undergo meiosis I to form two secondary spermatocytes; meiosis II then gives four spermatids, closer to the lumen.

Meiosis is reduction division: the chromosome number halves, so each gamete is haploid (23) and fertilisation restores the diploid number (46).

check.q: Which cell divides by meiosis I, and what does it produce?
check.a: The primary spermatocyte; two secondary spermatocytes.

steps.title: Spermiogenesis
steps.text:
Spermatogenesis is the whole journey from spermatogonium to sperm. Its last step, spermiogenesis, involves no division: each round spermatid sheds most of its cytoplasm, condenses its nucleus, builds an acrosome and grows a tail, becoming a spermatozoon released into the lumen.

Sperm leaving the testis still cannot fertilise; they mature further in the epididymis.

check.q: What is the difference between spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis?
check.a: Spermatogenesis is the whole process; spermiogenesis is the final remodelling of spermatids into sperm.

steps.title: Anatomy of a sperm
steps.text:
The sperm head holds the nucleus with its DNA, capped by the acrosome, a sac of digestive enzymes that lets the sperm penetrate the layers around the oocyte. A centriole sits at the neck.

The midpiece is packed with mitochondria that supply ATP, and the tail is a flagellum that propels the cell.

check.q: What does the acrosome contain, and why?
check.a: Digestive enzymes, to penetrate the coverings of the oocyte.

practice.q: Put spermatogenesis in order
Which cells form the blood–testis barrier?
practice.why: Tight junctions between Sertoli cells.

practice.q: Spermatids are:
practice.why: They are the products of meiosis II.

practice.q: What powers the sperm's flagellum?
practice.why: The midpiece mitochondria make ATP.

practice.q: Where are the spermatogonia, and how do they divide?
practice.a: Against the basement membrane of the tubule; by mitosis.

practice.q: Name the parts of a sperm and what each does.
practice.a: Head: nucleus (DNA) and acrosome (enzymes). Neck: centriole. Midpiece: mitochondria (ATP). Tail: flagellum (movement).

title: Epididymis, ductus deferens, spermatic cord and semen
summary: Where sperm mature, the route the ductus deferens takes through the groin, and who makes semen.
objectives: Describe the epididymis and its role
Trace the ductus deferens from the scrotum to the urethra
List the contents and coverings of the spermatic cord
State the contribution of each gland to semen
takeaways: Epididymis (head, body, tail): sperm stored and matured.
Ductus deferens: spermatic cord → inguinal canal → over the ureter → behind the bladder → ampulla.
Ductus deferens + seminal vesicle duct = ejaculatory duct, through the prostate.
Semen: seminal vesicles ~60%, prostate ~30%, sperm ~5%, bulbourethral mucus first.

steps.title: The epididymis
steps.text:
The epididymis caps the back of the testis: a head, body and tail built from one tightly coiled duct several metres long.

Sperm are stored here and mature, gaining the ability to swim. Sperm taken straight from the testis cannot fertilise; final capacitation happens in the female tract.

check.q: What happens to sperm in the epididymis?
check.a: They are stored and mature (gain motility).

steps.title: The route of the ductus deferens
steps.text:
The ductus (vas) deferens begins at the tail of the epididymis, climbs in the spermatic cord, passes through the inguinal canal into the pelvis, arches over the ureter and runs down behind the bladder. Its end widens as the ampulla.

There it joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct, which passes through the prostate into the urethra.

check.q: Which two ducts join to form the ejaculatory duct?
check.a: The ductus deferens (at its ampulla) and the duct of the seminal vesicle.

steps.title: The spermatic cord
steps.text:
The spermatic cord hangs each testis from the groin. It carries the ductus deferens, the testicular artery, the testicular veins (a network, the pampiniform plexus, that cools arterial blood), testicular nerves and lymphatics, with the cremaster muscle.

Its coats are the external spermatic fascia, cremaster muscle and fascia and internal spermatic fascia. It enters the inguinal canal at the superficial inguinal ring, above the inguinal ligament. The left cord is longer, so the left testis usually hangs lower.

check.q: List the contents of the spermatic cord.
check.a: Ductus deferens, testicular artery, testicular veins (pampiniform plexus), nerves, lymphatics and the cremaster muscle.

steps.title: Glands and semen
steps.text:
Seminal fluid is the glands' secretion; semen is that fluid plus sperm. The seminal vesicles supply about 60% of its volume, an alkaline fluid rich in fructose. The prostate, just below the bladder around the prostatic urethra, adds about 30%, a milky, slightly alkaline buffer.

Sperm themselves are only about 5%. Before ejaculation the bulbourethral glands beside the membranous urethra release lubricating mucus (pre-ejaculate).

check.q: Which gland contributes most of the semen volume?
check.a: The seminal vesicles (about 60%).

practice.q: List the spermatic cord coverings from outside in
About what share of semen volume do sperm make up?
practice.why: Most volume comes from the seminal vesicles and prostate.

practice.q: The ductus deferens passes:
choices: Over the ureter, behind the bladder
practice.why: It loops over the ureter to reach the back of the bladder.

practice.q: What is the difference between seminal fluid and semen?
practice.a: Seminal fluid is the glandular secretion; semen is seminal fluid plus sperm.

practice.q: Why does the left testis usually hang lower?
practice.a: The left spermatic cord is longer.

title: Penis, male urethra and perineum
summary: Three parts of urethra, three erectile cylinders, and the diamond-shaped floor between the thighs.
objectives: Name the three parts of the male urethra
Describe the parts and erectile bodies of the penis and its root
Identify the dorsal vessels, nerve and fasciae in cross-section and explain erection
Describe the boundaries and triangles of the perineum
takeaways: Prostatic → membranous → spongy urethra → external urethral orifice on the glans.
Two dorsal corpora cavernosa; one ventral corpus spongiosum (glans in front, bulb behind).
Root of penis = crura (covered by ischiocavernosus) + bulb.
Perineum: urogenital triangle in front, anal triangle behind, split by a line between the ischial tuberosities.

steps.title: Three parts of urethra
steps.text: The male urethra has three parts. The prostatic urethra runs through the prostate; the short membranous urethra crosses the pelvic floor (urogenital diaphragm); the long spongy (penile) urethra runs through the corpus spongiosum to the external urethral orifice on the glans.

check.q: Which part of the male urethra lies in the corpus spongiosum?
check.a: The spongy (penile) urethra.

steps.title: Body, glans and root
steps.text:
The penis has a shaft (body), an expanded tip, the glans penis, and a skin fold, the prepuce (foreskin), which is removed in circumcision. The frenulum underneath is rich in nerve endings.

Three cylinders of erectile tissue run along it: two dorsal corpora cavernosa and one ventral corpus spongiosum around the urethra. The spongiosum expands as the glans in front and the bulb behind; the cavernosa diverge as the crura, covered by ischiocavernosus. Crura and bulb form the root, anchored to the pubic arch.

check.q: Which erectile body contains the urethra?
check.a: The corpus spongiosum.

steps.title: Cross-section and erection
steps.text:
A cross-section shows, in the dorsal midline, the deep dorsal vein flanked by the dorsal arteries and dorsal nerves, all under the deep fascia; the superficial dorsal vein lies in the superficial fascia beneath the skin.

In erection, the arterioles dilate and the erectile tissue fills with blood, which compresses the veins draining it; it subsides when the arteries constrict again. Average erect length is about 13–16 cm.

check.q: What causes erection?
check.a: Arteriolar dilation fills the erectile tissue with blood, which compresses the outflow veins.

steps.title: The perineum
steps.text:
The perineum is the diamond-shaped region of the pelvic outlet, between the pubic symphysis in front, the ischial tuberosities at the sides and the coccyx behind.

A line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into the anterior urogenital triangle (external genitalia) and the posterior anal triangle (anus). Clinically, 'the perineum' often means just the small area between the scrotum or vaginal opening and the anus.

check.q: Which landmarks bound the perineum?
check.a: Pubic symphysis, both ischial tuberosities and the coccyx.

practice.q: Put the male urethra in order
The root of the penis consists of:
practice.why: Anchored to the pubic arch and perineum.

practice.q: What is removed in circumcision?
practice.a: The prepuce (foreskin).

practice.q: What does each triangle of the perineum contain?
practice.a: Urogenital triangle: the external genitalia. Anal triangle: the anus.

practice.q: Name the structures in the dorsal midline of the penis from superficial to deep.
practice.a: Skin, superficial fascia with the superficial dorsal vein, deep fascia, then the deep dorsal vein with dorsal arteries and nerves on either side.

title: The female system and the ovary
summary: Organs of the female tract, the layers of the ovary, and a follicle's life from primordial to scar.
objectives: List the organs of the female reproductive system
Describe the layers of the ovary
Put the follicle stages in order and describe each
Describe ovulation, the corpus luteum and the corpus albicans
takeaways: Ovaries, uterine tubes, uterus, vagina, vulva, mammary glands.
Ovary: germinal epithelium, tunica albuginea, cortex (follicles), medulla (vessels).
Primordial → primary → secondary → mature (Graafian) follicle → ovulation → corpus luteum → corpus albicans.
Ovulation releases a secondary oocyte with its zona pellucida and corona radiata.

steps.title: The female tract
steps.text:
The female system is the ovaries (gonads), uterine tubes, uterus, vagina, the external genitalia (vulva) and the mammary glands. The atlas body is male, so the female organs are shown in the female reproductive model.

Each ovary is an almond-sized oval, about 3–4 cm long, in the peritoneal cavity. It is not joined to its uterine tube: at ovulation the oocyte is shed from its surface and must be swept into the tube.

check.q: Is the ovary attached to the uterine tube?
check.a: No: the oocyte is released into the peritoneal cavity and swept into the tube by the fimbriae.

steps.title: Layers of the ovary
steps.text: The ovary is covered by visceral peritoneum, historically called the germinal epithelium. Under it is a fibrous capsule, the tunica albuginea. The outer cortex holds the follicles; the inner medulla carries the blood vessels. The connective tissue of both is the stroma.

check.q: Which region of the ovary holds the follicles?
check.a: The cortex.

steps.title: A follicle grows
steps.text:
A primordial follicle is a primary oocyte in a single layer of flat follicular cells. In a primary follicle they become cuboidal granulosa cells and the zona pellucida forms around the oocyte. A secondary follicle develops fluid-filled vesicles and a theca.

The mature (Graafian, vesicular) follicle has one large antrum, the oocyte perched on the cumulus oophorus, and a theca interna and externa. By now its oocyte has finished meiosis I and is a secondary oocyte.

check.q: What fills the antrum, and which follicle has a single large one?
check.a: Follicular fluid; the mature (Graafian) follicle.

steps.title: Ovulation and after
steps.text:
At ovulation the follicle ruptures and releases the secondary oocyte, still wrapped in its zona pellucida and a halo of granulosa cells, the corona radiata. Humans usually release one; cats release several.

The granulosa cells left behind become the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone (and estrogen). Without pregnancy it degenerates into a white scar, the corpus albicans. Most follicles never ovulate and degenerate as atretic follicles. This whole production of female gametes is oogenesis.

check.q: What does the corpus luteum secrete, and what does it become without pregnancy?
check.a: Progesterone (and estrogen); it degenerates into the corpus albicans.

practice.q: Put the ovarian follicle stages in order
A primordial follicle contains:
choices: A primary oocyte in flat follicular cells
A secondary oocyte on a cumulus
practice.why: Granulosa cells become cuboidal in the primary follicle.

practice.q: Which follicle stage first shows fluid-filled vesicles and a theca?
practice.why: The vesicles merge into one antrum in the mature follicle.

practice.q: What is released at ovulation?
choices: Secondary oocyte with zona pellucida and corona radiata
practice.why: Meiosis II finishes only if a sperm enters.

practice.q: Name the layers of the ovary from outside in.
practice.a: Visceral peritoneum (germinal epithelium), tunica albuginea, cortex, medulla.

practice.q: What is an atretic follicle?
practice.a: A degenerating follicle that will not ovulate.

practice.q: What is the cumulus oophorus?
practice.a: The mound of granulosa cells on which the oocyte sits in a mature follicle.

practice.q: What is oogenesis?
practice.a: The production of female gametes (oocytes/ova) in the ovary.

title: Uterine tubes, uterus and vagina
summary: Four parts of tube, four parts of uterus, three layers of uterine wall and a stretchy vagina.
objectives: Name the parts of the uterine tube and where fertilisation occurs
Name the regions and openings of the uterus
Describe the layers of the uterine wall and the two layers of endometrium
Describe the vagina
takeaways: Tube: fimbriae/infundibulum → ampulla (fertilisation) → isthmus → uterine part.
Uterus: fundus, body, isthmus, cervix (cervical canal, external os).
Perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium; the functional layer is shed, the basal layer regrows it.
Vagina: non-keratinised stratified squamous, rugae, fornix around the cervix.

steps.title: The uterine tube
steps.text:
Each uterine (fallopian) tube, or oviduct, starts as a funnel, the infundibulum, fringed by finger-like fimbriae around its opening (ostium) near the ovary. Next is the wide ampulla, the usual site of fertilisation, then the narrow isthmus, and finally the uterine (intramural) part in the uterine wall.

Its wall has a ciliated mucosa, a muscular layer and a serosa; the mesosalpinx suspends it.

check.q: Where does fertilisation usually happen?
check.a: In the ampulla of the uterine tube.

steps.title: Regions of the uterus
steps.text:
The uterus is pear-shaped. The fundus is the dome above the entry of the tubes; below is the body, then a short constricted isthmus, and the cervix, which projects into the vagina.

The uterine cavity narrows into the cervical canal, which opens into the vagina at the external os. A Pap smear scrapes cells from the cervix to screen for cancer and precancerous change.

check.q: What is a Pap smear?
check.a: A scraping of cervical cells examined for cancer or precancerous change.

steps.title: The uterine wall
steps.text:
Outside is the perimetrium, a serosa. The thick middle myometrium is smooth muscle that contracts in labour. The inner mucosa is the endometrium.

The endometrium has a functional layer, with coiled uterine glands and spiral arteries, that thickens each cycle and is shed at menstruation; and a thin basal layer, supplied by straight arteries, which survives and regenerates the functional layer.

check.q: Which layer of endometrium is shed at menstruation, and which regrows it?
check.a: The functional layer is shed; the basal layer regenerates it.

steps.title: The vagina
steps.text:
The vagina runs from the cervix to the vaginal opening, which lies between the urethral opening in front and the anus behind. Around the cervix it forms a recess, the fornix; its walls carry transverse ridges, rugae.

It is lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, is poorly innervated, and stretches greatly in childbirth. A thin fold, the hymen, may partly surround the opening.

check.q: What is the vaginal fornix?
check.a: The recess of the vagina around the projecting cervix.

practice.q: Put the uterine tube in order from ovary to uterus
Put the uterus in order from top to bottom
The myometrium is:
practice.why: It contracts in labour.

practice.q: Which arteries supply the functional and basal layers of the endometrium?
practice.a: Spiral arteries (functional layer); straight arteries (basal layer).

practice.q: Name the three layers of the uterine tube wall.
practice.a: Ciliated mucosa, muscular layer, serosa.

practice.q: What lines the vagina?
practice.a: Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.

practice.q: What is the external os?
practice.a: The opening of the cervical canal into the vagina.

title: External genitalia and the supporting ligaments
summary: The vulva from the mons to the perineum, homologues of the male organs, and four ligaments.
objectives: Name the parts of the vulva and their male homologues
Put the openings of the vestibule in order
Name the broad ligament's parts and the round, ovarian and suspensory ligaments
takeaways: Mons pubis, labia majora (≈ scrotum), labia minora, clitoris (≈ penis).
Vestibule, front to back: clitoris, urethral opening, vaginal opening; Bartholin glands behind.
Broad ligament = mesometrium + mesosalpinx + mesovarium.
Round ligament: uterus → inguinal canal → labia majora. Ovarian ligament: ovary → uterus. Suspensory ligament: ovary → pelvic wall, carrying ovarian vessels.

steps.title: The vulva
steps.text:
The vulva is the female external genitalia. The mons pubis is a fat pad over the pubic symphysis. Below it the labia majora — the homologue of the scrotum — enclose the pudendal cleft; inside them lie the thinner labia minora.

The clitoris is erectile tissue with a body and glans, the homologue of the penis, richly supplied with nerve endings; the labia minora meet over it as its prepuce.

check.q: What are the male homologues of the clitoris and labia majora?
check.a: The penis and the scrotum.

steps.title: The vestibule
steps.text:
The vestibule is the space between the labia minora. From front to back it contains the clitoris, the urethral opening and the vaginal opening. The greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands open posterolaterally and lubricate it.

The hymen, a fold of mucous membrane partly around the vaginal opening, varies greatly and is not a reliable sign of virginity. Behind lies the clinical perineum.

check.q: Put the openings in the vestibule in order from front to back.
check.a: Clitoris, urethral opening, vaginal opening.

steps.title: Ligaments that hold the organs
steps.text:
The broad ligament is a sheet of peritoneum draped over the uterus, tubes and ovaries. Its parts are the mesometrium (beside the uterus), mesosalpinx (under the tube) and mesovarium (holding the ovary).

The round ligament runs from the uterus through the inguinal canal to the labia majora. The ovarian ligament ties the ovary to the uterus, and the suspensory ligament ties it to the lateral pelvic wall, carrying the ovarian vessels.

check.q: Which ligament carries the ovarian vessels?
check.a: The suspensory ligament of the ovary.

practice.q: Put the vestibule in order from anterior to posterior
Where does the round ligament of the uterus end?
practice.why: It passes through the inguinal canal.

practice.q: What is the pudendal cleft?
practice.a: The slit between the labia majora.

practice.q: Is the hymen a reliable indicator of virginity?
practice.a: No; it varies greatly and can stretch or tear for many reasons.

title: The ovarian and menstrual cycles
summary: Four hormones, two linked cycles and one 28-day calendar.
objectives: Describe the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis
Relate the follicular and luteal phases to the menstrual, proliferative and secretory phases
Explain the LH surge, menstruation and negative feedback
takeaways: GnRH (hypothalamus) → FSH and LH (anterior pituitary) → ovary.
Days 1–5 menses; 6–14 proliferative (estrogen); ovulation ~day 14 after the LH surge; 15–28 secretory (progesterone).
Falling estrogen and progesterone as the corpus luteum dies → functional layer sloughs.
High estrogen and progesterone suppress FSH and LH by negative feedback.

steps.title: The control axis
steps.text:
The hypothalamus releases GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone), which drives the anterior pituitary to release FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) and LH (luteinizing hormone).

These act on the ovary, and the ovary's hormones, estrogen and progesterone, act on the uterus. The ovarian cycle and the menstrual (uterine) cycle therefore run in step, over about 28 days.

check.q: Which gland releases FSH and LH, and what stimulates it?
check.a: The anterior pituitary, stimulated by GnRH from the hypothalamus.

steps.title: Days 1–14: menses and the follicular phase
steps.text:
Day 1 is the first day of menses (menstruation), which lasts about 5 days. Meanwhile FSH stimulates a group of follicles to grow and secrete estrogen: the ovary's follicular phase.

Rising estrogen rebuilds the functional layer of the endometrium in the proliferative phase, about days 6–14.

check.q: Which hormone drives the proliferative phase?
check.a: Estrogen from the growing follicles.

steps.title: Ovulation and the luteal phase
steps.text:
Estrogen peaks just before mid-cycle and triggers an LH surge, which causes ovulation at about day 14 and turns the ruptured follicle into the corpus luteum.

In the luteal phase the corpus luteum secretes progesterone (with some estrogen). Progesterone makes the endometrial glands coil and secrete — the secretory phase, days 15–28 — ready for an embryo.

check.q: What triggers ovulation?
check.a: The LH surge, around day 14.

steps.title: Menstruation and negative feedback
steps.text:
If no pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum degenerates from about day 25. Estrogen and progesterone fall, the spiral arteries constrict, and the functional layer sloughs away: menstruation, day 1 of the next cycle.

Through most of the cycle, high estrogen and progesterone suppress FSH and LH by negative feedback. That is the basis of hormonal contraception.

check.q: Why does menstruation start?
check.a: The corpus luteum degenerates, so estrogen and progesterone fall and the functional layer is shed.

practice.q: Put the menstrual cycle in order starting at day 1
Put the hormonal sequence in order
Which hormone dominates the secretory phase?
practice.why: Secreted by the corpus luteum.

practice.q: The follicular phase of the ovary coincides with which uterine phases?
practice.why: The luteal phase coincides with the secretory phase.

practice.q: What does LH stand for?
practice.why: It forms the corpus luteum.

practice.q: What is negative feedback in the cycle?
practice.a: High estrogen and progesterone inhibit GnRH, FSH and LH release.

practice.q: What does FSH do?
practice.a: Stimulates follicle growth and estrogen secretion.

title: Contraception
summary: Blocking the gametes, cutting the ducts, or switching off ovulation.
objectives: Classify contraceptive methods by how they work
Describe vasectomy and tubal ligation anatomically
Explain how hormonal contraception and mifepristone act
takeaways: Abstention is the only completely effective method.
Barrier methods (condom, diaphragm, spermicidal foam) keep sperm from the oocyte.
Vasectomy cuts the ductus deferens; tubal ligation cuts the uterine tubes.
Estrogen + progestin pills and progesterone implants stop ovulation by negative feedback.

steps.title: Keeping gametes apart
steps.text:
Abstention is the only completely effective method. A condom is a barrier over the penis. A diaphragm is a rubber dome over the cervix, used with spermicidal foam or gel that kills sperm.

Coitus interruptus (withdrawal) is unreliable because the pre-ejaculate can already carry sperm.

check.q: Why is withdrawal unreliable?
check.a: Sperm may already be present in the pre-ejaculate.

steps.title: Sterilisation
steps.text:
In vasectomy (male sterilisation), each ductus deferens is cut and tied through a small incision in the scrotum. Sperm are still made but are reabsorbed; the glands still produce ejaculate, and erection is unaffected.

In tubal ligation each uterine tube is cut and tied, so sperm and oocyte cannot meet.

check.q: Does vasectomy affect erection or ejaculation?
check.a: No: erection is unaffected and the glands still produce ejaculate, just without sperm.

steps.title: Hormonal methods
steps.text:
Oral contraceptives contain synthetic estrogen and a progestin. By negative feedback they suppress FSH and LH, so no follicle matures and no LH surge triggers ovulation. Progesterone implants under the skin also prevent ovulation.

Mifepristone is an antiprogesterone: it blocks progesterone's support of the endometrium and so ends an early pregnancy.

check.q: How do combined oral contraceptives prevent ovulation?
check.a: Estrogen and progestin suppress FSH and LH by negative feedback, so there is no LH surge.

practice.q: Which method is completely effective?
practice.why: No contact, no fertilisation.

practice.q: In vasectomy, which structure is cut?
practice.why: Through a small scrotal incision.

practice.q: Mifepristone acts by:
practice.why: It is an antiprogesterone.

practice.q: What is tubal ligation?
practice.a: Cutting and tying the uterine tubes (female sterilisation).

practice.q: Name two barrier methods.
practice.a: Condom; diaphragm (with spermicidal foam).

practice.q: How does a progesterone implant work?
practice.a: It releases progestin that suppresses ovulation.

title: The breast
summary: Modified sweat glands: surface features, the lobes inside, and the path milk takes to the nipple.
objectives: Name the surface features of the breast
Describe the internal structure and the path of milk
Contrast the lactating and non-lactating breast
takeaways: Mammary glands are modified sweat glands.
Nipple, areola with areolar glands, axillary tail (of Spence) — a common tumour site.
15–20 lobes → lobules of alveolar glands → lactiferous ducts → lactiferous sinus → nipple.
Suspensory ligaments anchor the breast to the pectoral fascia over pectoralis major.

steps.title: Surface of the breast
steps.text:
The mammary glands are modified sweat glands of the skin, counted as accessory reproductive organs because they nourish the young. Each breast has a body, a central nipple, and a pigmented areola dotted with bumps made by the areolar glands.

An axillary tail (tail of Spence) extends toward the armpit — a common site for tumours — and a smaller lateral process reaches sideways.

check.q: Why does breast examination include the armpit?
check.a: The axillary tail (of Spence) extends into it and is a common tumour site.

steps.title: Inside: lobes and ducts
steps.text:
Each breast holds 15–20 lobes, each divided into lobules of milk-secreting alveolar glands, all embedded in adipose tissue. Milk flows from the glands into lactiferous ducts, which widen into a lactiferous sinus (ampulla) before opening on the nipple — many openings in humans, a single one in a cow's teat.

Suspensory ligaments run from the skin to the pectoral fascia over pectoralis major, with the ribs beneath.

check.q: Trace milk from the gland to the nipple.
check.a: Alveolar glands of a lobule → lactiferous duct → lactiferous sinus → nipple opening.

steps.title: Lactating and non-lactating
steps.text:
In the non-lactating breast the glands are small and scattered in fat and fibrous tissue. During pregnancy they multiply and enlarge, and they become fully functional after delivery: lactation, or milk production.

A cat has several pairs of mammary glands along the ventral body wall, one set for each of its many young.

check.q: How does a lactating breast differ on a slide?
check.a: Its glands are enlarged and numerous with milk in the lumens; a non-lactating breast is mostly fat and fibrous tissue with few small ducts.

practice.q: Trace milk to the surface
Mammary glands are modified:
practice.why: They develop from the skin.

practice.q: How many lobes does a breast have?
practice.why: Each is subdivided into lobules.

practice.q: What anchors the breast to the chest wall?
practice.a: Suspensory (Cooper) ligaments attached to the pectoral fascia over pectoralis major.

practice.q: What is the tail of Spence, and why is it important?
practice.a: The axillary tail of the breast; a common site of breast tumours.

practice.q: What makes the bumps on the areola?
practice.a: Areolar glands.

practice.q: What is the lateral process of the breast?
practice.a: A small extension of the breast tissue toward the side of the chest.

title: Fertilisation and the first weeks
summary: From two pronuclei in the tube to an implanted blastocyst with three germ layers.
objectives: Describe fertilisation and the zygote
Put cleavage, morula and blastocyst in order and describe each
Describe implantation and the early membranes
Name the three germ layers and what each forms
takeaways: Fertilisation in the ampulla: sperm and egg pronuclei fuse into a zygote.
Cleavage (2, 4, 8, 16 cells) → morula (solid) → blastocyst (trophoblast, inner cell mass, blastocele).
Implantation ~day 7; amniotic cavity above and yolk sac below the embryonic disk.
Ectoderm: skin, nervous tissue. Mesoderm: bone, muscle, blood. Endoderm: gut and airway linings.

steps.title: Fertilisation
steps.text:
Fertilisation usually happens in the ampulla of the uterine tube. Enzymes from many sperm acrosomes clear a path through the corona radiata and zona pellucida, and one sperm enters the secondary oocyte, which then completes meiosis II and becomes the ovum.

The egg pronucleus and sperm pronucleus fuse, restoring the diploid number: the single cell is now a zygote.

check.q: What is a zygote?
check.a: The single diploid cell formed when the egg and sperm pronuclei fuse.

steps.title: Cleavage and the morula
steps.text:
As it travels down the tube the zygote divides by cleavage: 2-, 4-, 8- and 16-cell stages. The cells get smaller with each division; the whole ball does not grow.

By about day 3–4 it is a solid ball of cells, the morula ('mulberry'), arriving in the uterus.

check.q: Does the embryo grow during cleavage?
check.a: No: the cells divide and get smaller; overall size stays about the same.

steps.title: Blastocyst and implantation
steps.text:
Fluid gathers inside to form a hollow blastocyst: an outer layer, the trophoblast, which will form part of the placenta; a cluster inside, the inner cell mass, which becomes the embryo; and a cavity, the blastocele.

Around day 7 the blastocyst implants: the trophoblast invades through the uterine epithelium into the secretory endometrium.

check.q: Which part of the blastocyst becomes the embryo, and which helps form the placenta?
check.a: Inner cell mass → embryo; trophoblast → part of the placenta.

steps.title: Membranes, stalk and placenta
steps.text:
In the second week the inner cell mass flattens into a two-layered embryonic disk (ectoderm and endoderm). Above it opens the amniotic cavity, lined by the amnion (amniotic sac); below hangs the yolk sac.

A connecting stalk joins the disk to the trophoblast and becomes the umbilical cord, linking the embryo (later the fetus, from week 9) to the placenta.

check.q: What does the connecting stalk become?
check.a: The umbilical cord.

steps.title: Three germ layers
steps.text:
In week three a third layer forms between the two, giving the primary germ layers.

Ectoderm (outer) forms the epidermis of the skin, the nervous tissue and the adrenal medulla. Mesoderm (middle) forms bone, muscle, blood, connective tissue and the kidneys. Endoderm (inner) forms the lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts and the organs that grow from them.

check.q: Which germ layer forms nervous tissue, and which the lining of the gut?
check.a: Ectoderm forms nervous tissue; endoderm lines the gut.

practice.q: Put early development in order
Which germ layer forms bone and muscle?
practice.why: Mesoderm also forms blood and the kidneys.

practice.q: Which germ layer forms the epidermis and adrenal medulla?
practice.why: Nervous tissue is ectoderm too.

practice.q: Where does implantation happen, and when?
practice.why: The blastocyst reaches the uterus as a morula/early blastocyst.

practice.q: Name the three parts of a blastocyst.
practice.a: Trophoblast, inner cell mass, blastocele.

practice.q: Which structures lie above and below the embryonic disk?
practice.a: Amniotic cavity (amnion) above; yolk sac below.

practice.q: What does endoderm form?
practice.a: The lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts and their associated organs.

practice.q: When does an embryo become a fetus?
practice.a: From about week 9.

title: The cat reproductive system
summary: What a dissected cat shows: no seminal vesicles, a barbed penis, a Y-shaped uterus and a litter.
objectives: Compare the male cat's ducts and glands with the human
Describe the female cat's ovaries, tubes, bicornuate uterus and urogenital sinus
Describe what a pregnant cat shows
takeaways: Male cat: no seminal vesicles; single prostate, paired bulbourethral glands; barbed penis.
Female cat: bicornuate uterus with two horns; vagina and urethra join in a urogenital sinus.
Each kitten has its own placenta and umbilical cord in the uterine horn.

steps.title: The male cat
steps.text:
An intact tom has a scrotum with two testes (absent if neutered), each in a tunica vaginalis with its epididymis. The ductus deferens runs in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal, then loops over the ureter dorsal to the bladder. The pelvic organs are reached by cutting through the pubic symphysis in the midline.

Differences: a single prostate, paired bulbourethral glands, no seminal vesicles, and a penis with keratinised backward-pointing barbs that help induce ovulation, inside a prepuce.

check.q: Which human accessory gland does the cat lack?
check.a: The seminal vesicles.

steps.title: The female cat
steps.text:
The small ovaries lie just caudal to the kidneys. Short uterine tubes (oviducts) curl around them, each with an ostium, infundibulum and fimbriae. The uterus is bicornuate: two long uterine horns join a short body, a Y shape suited to carrying a litter. A cervix leads to the vagina.

The vagina and urethra join in a vaginal vestibule (urogenital sinus) that opens at a single urogenital opening. The mesovarium, mesosalpinx, mesometrium and round ligament are all present.

check.q: What is a bicornuate uterus?
check.a: A uterus with two long horns joined to a short body (Y-shaped).

steps.title: The pregnant cat
steps.text:
Cats release several oocytes at a time. A pregnant cat's uterine horns bulge with evenly spaced swellings, one per kitten; each fetus lies in its own sac with its own placenta and umbilical cord.

Several pairs of mammary glands along the ventral body will feed the litter.

check.q: What links each kitten to its placenta?
check.a: Its umbilical cord.

practice.q: How does the cat uterus differ from the human uterus?
practice.why: The horns carry the litter.

practice.q: In the female cat, the urethra opens into:
practice.why: Human females have separate urethral and vaginal openings.

practice.q: What is unusual about the cat penis?
practice.why: The barbs help induce ovulation.

practice.q: Where are the cat's ovaries?
practice.a: Just caudal to the kidneys.

practice.q: How are the pelvic organs of a cat exposed?
practice.a: By a midsagittal cut through the pubic symphysis.

practice.q: Which structures of a male cat disappear after neutering?
practice.a: The testes (and scrotal contents).

practice.q: What do the cat's short uterine tubes (oviducts) end in near the ovary?
practice.a: An ostium in an infundibulum fringed by fimbriae.
